title: Copying nature
text: In 1941, a Swiss engineer called George de Mestral returned from a walk in the mountains with his dog and noticed that both his trousers and the fur of the dog were covered in burrs, the small seed heads of a common plant. Most people would simply have pulled them off and thrown them away. De Mestral, however, was curious. He put one under a microscope and discovered that it was covered in hundreds of tiny hooks, which caught on anything with loops, such as fabric or hair.

It took him years of experiments to copy the idea, but the result was Velcro, a fastener made of two strips of material, one with hooks and the other with loops. At first, the fashion industry was not impressed, and some people thought it looked cheap. Its big break came when space agencies began to use it, because it allowed astronauts to fix objects to the walls so that they would not float away. Today it can be found on everything from trainers to medical equipment.

De Mestral was not the first person to learn from nature, and he certainly was not the last. The practice of solving human problems by copying solutions from living things now has a name: biomimicry. Its supporters point out that plants and animals have had millions of years of evolution to test their designs, so it would be foolish not to learn from them.

One of the most famous examples comes from Japan. In the nineteen nineties, engineers working on the bullet train faced a serious problem. Whenever the train came out of a tunnel at high speed, it pushed a wave of air in front of it, causing a loud bang that disturbed people living nearby. The solution came from an engineer who was also a keen birdwatcher. He knew that the kingfisher dives into water to catch fish with hardly a splash, thanks to its long, narrow beak. When the front of the train was redesigned in the shape of that beak, the noise was reduced, and the train used less electricity too.

Other examples are just as clever. The leaves of the lotus plant always stay clean because their surface is covered in tiny bumps that make water roll off, taking the dirt with it. This discovery has inspired self-cleaning paints and glass. Termite mounds in Africa, which stay cool even in extreme heat thanks to a system of tunnels that let air flow through them, have influenced the design of buildings that need much less air conditioning.

Not every attempt to copy nature is successful, of course. Living things are incredibly complex, and what works for an insect does not always work on a human scale. Some designs that seem brilliant in a laboratory turn out to be too expensive to produce. Nevertheless, as engineers search for ways to use less energy and fewer resources, interest in biomimicry is growing fast.

Perhaps the most important lesson is the one de Mestral learnt on his walk. Great ideas are not always the result of complicated research. Sometimes they are stuck to your trousers, waiting for someone curious enough to take a closer look.

He had a microscope at home.

According to the third paragraph, why should we learn from nature?
Evolution has finished testing all designs.
Nature has tested its designs over a very long time.
Copying nature is cheaper than research.
Animals are more intelligent than engineers.
What problem did the engineers in Japan need to solve?
The train made a loud noise when it left a tunnel.
The train used too much water.
Birds were flying into the train.
The train was too slow in tunnels.
What do the lotus plant and termite mounds have in common in the fifth paragraph?
They are both found only in Africa.
They both use water to stay cool.
They have both inspired useful products or buildings.
They both have surfaces with tiny hooks.
What is the writer suggesting in the last sentence?
Complicated research is a waste of time.
People should clean their trousers after a walk.
Only engineers can have great ideas.
Good ideas can come from paying attention to ordinary things.

parts.title: Part 1 · Multiple-choice cloze

parts.text: Many of the objects we use every day were invented {{0}} accident. The microwave oven is a good example. parts.title: Part 2 · Open cloze
parts.help: Write one word in each gap.
parts.text: Biomimicry is not a new idea. More than five hundred years {{6}}, Leonardo da Vinci studied birds in the hope {{7}} building a flying machine. Although his designs never left the ground, they showed that he understood how important it was to observe nature closely. Today, engineers have tools {{8}} Leonardo could only dream of. Computers allow them to study the movement of a fish or the structure of a leaf in incredible detail. As a {{9}}, the number of inventions inspired by nature has grown rapidly. {{10}} knows what the next one will be? It could {{11}} waiting in your garden right now.

parts.title: Part 3 · Word formation
parts.help: Use the word in capitals at the end of each gap to form a word that fits.
parts.text: George de Mestral was a {{12}} engineer. His {{13}} was not successful at first, but he never gave up. Today, Velcro is used by millions of people for its {{14}}. Biomimicry shows that nature can be a {{15}} source of ideas. Many {{16}} advances have come from careful {{17}} of plants and animals.
